topics.title: JSX
topics.content: JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML and works inside JavaScript. It allows you to describe the UI structure in a familiar way while still using JavaScript expressions.

questions.question: What is JSX?
questions.answer: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript used in React to describe UI structure with HTML-like syntax.

questions.question: Can JSX contain JavaScript expressions?
questions.answer: Yes, you can include JavaScript expressions inside JSX using curly braces, such as {user.name}.

questions.question: test
questions.answer: testu

topics.title: Components
topics.content: React components are reusable pieces of UI. A component can be a function that returns JSX, making it easy to build complex interfaces from simple building blocks.

questions.question: What is a React component?
questions.answer: A React component is a reusable UI element that can be defined as a function or class and returns JSX.

questions.question: What is the difference between function and class components?
questions.answer: Function components are simpler and support hooks, while class components use lifecycle methods and state with this.state. Modern React prefers function components.

topics.title: Props
topics.content: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child. They are read-only and allow components to receive dynamic data and render it accordingly.

questions.question: What are props in React?
questions.answer: Props are read-only values passed from a parent component to a child component to configure it.

questions.question: Can props be modified inside a component?
questions.answer: No, props are immutable inside the receiving component and should not be changed.

topics.title: State
topics.content: State is internal component data that can change over time. Updating state causes React to re-render the component with the new values.
topics.example: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>; }

questions.question: What is state in React?
questions.answer: State is internal data managed by a component that can change over time and drives re-rendering.

questions.question: How do you update state in a functional component?
questions.answer: Use the setter function returned by useState, such as setCount(newValue).

topics.title: Event Handling
topics.content: React handles events with camelCase props like onClick and onChange. You pass event handler functions to respond when the user interacts with the UI.
topics.example: function Button() { const handleClick = () => alert('Clicked!'); return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>; }

questions.question: How do you handle events in React?
questions.answer: Use event handler props like onClick or onChange and pass a function reference to them.

questions.question: Why is the event name camelCase in React?
questions.answer: React uses camelCase for event handlers to match JavaScript naming conventions.

topics.title: useEffect
topics.content: useEffect runs code after the component renders. It is used for side effects such as fetching data, updating the DOM, or subscribing to events.

questions.question: What does useEffect do?
questions.answer: useEffect runs side effects after render and can clean up when dependencies change or the component unmounts.

questions.question: When does useEffect run?
questions.answer: It runs after the component renders and whenever its dependency array values change.

topics.title: useState
topics.content: useState lets functional components have local state. It returns a state value and a setter function to update that value.

questions.question: What does useState return?
questions.answer: useState returns a state value and a setter function to update it.

questions.question: Can you update state directly?
questions.answer: No, you should use the setter function returned by useState rather than mutating the state directly.

topics.title: useReducer
topics.content: useReducer is a hook for managing complex state logic. It is useful when the next state depends on the previous state or when handling multiple state values together.

questions.question: When should you use useReducer?
questions.answer: Use useReducer for complex state logic or when state transitions are easier to express with actions and a reducer.

questions.question: What are the two values returned by useReducer?
questions.answer: It returns the current state and a dispatch function to send actions.

topics.title: Dot Net Overview
topics.content: The .NET platform is a developer platform for building many types of applications. It supports languages like C#, F#, and Visual Basic.
topics.example:
using System;
class Program { static void Main() { Console.WriteLine("Hello from .NET"); } }

questions.question: What is .NET?
questions.answer: .NET is a free, cross-platform, open source developer platform for building many types of applications.

topics.title: Runtime and Framework
topics.content: The .NET runtime executes managed code and includes services like garbage collection and assembly loading.
topics.example: // .NET code compiled to IL runs on the CLR runtime.

questions.question: What is the CLR in .NET?
questions.answer: The CLR is the Common Language Runtime that executes managed .NET code and provides services such as garbage collection.

topics.title: Cross-platform .NET Core
topics.content: .NET Core is a cross-platform implementation of .NET that runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
topics.example:
dotnet new console -n MyApp
dotnet run --project MyApp

questions.question: What is .NET Core?
questions.answer: .NET Core is a cross-platform implementation of .NET for building console, web, and cloud apps.

topics.title: Performance and Deployment
topics.content: .NET Core is optimized for performance and supports lightweight deployment models like self-contained and framework-dependent apps.
topics.example: Publish with dotnet publish -c Release to create distributable app files.

questions.question: How do you publish a .NET Core app?
questions.answer: Use dotnet publish -c Release to create deployable output for your app.

topics.title: API Basics
topics.content: An API is a set of rules that lets different software systems communicate with each other.
topics.example: GET /api/products returns a list of product data in JSON format.

questions.question: What is an API?
questions.answer: An API is an application programming interface that allows applications to talk to each other.

topics.title: RESTful API Design
topics.content: RESTful APIs use HTTP verbs like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to manage resources.
topics.example: POST /api/users with user data creates a new user record.

questions.question: What does REST stand for?
questions.answer: REST stands for Representational State Transfer and is a common pattern for designing web APIs.
